nameStory: The round-tipped conehead gets its name from the distinctive cone-shaped projection on top of its head, which has a blunt, rounded tip rather than a sharp point. This 'cone' is actually part of their head structure called the fastigium, and it's one of the easiest ways to tell different conehead species apart in the field.
description: Round-tipped coneheads are medium-sized katydids that belong to the grasshopper and cricket family (Orthoptera). These slender, green insects measure about 1.5 to 2 inches long and have long, thread-like antennae that can be twice as long as their bodies. Like other katydids, they're excellent jumpers with powerful hind legs, and males produce their characteristic chirping songs by rubbing their wings together. You'll most often spot these musical insects during late summer and early fall in grassy, weedy areas.

idTips.label: Cone-shaped head projection
idTips.description: Look for the blunt, rounded cone on top of the head between the eyes - it feels firm to the touch and doesn't come to a sharp point like some relatives

idTips.label: Body size and color
idTips.description: Bright green body about 1.5-2 inches long with a slender build; feels smooth and somewhat delicate when gently handled

idTips.label: Extra-long antennae
idTips.description: Thread-thin antennae that extend far beyond the body length, constantly moving and twitching as they explore their surroundings

idTips.label: Powerful hind legs
idTips.description: Enlarged jumping legs with visible spines along the sides that feel rough and sturdy compared to the smooth body

idTips.label: Wing position
idTips.description: Wings held roof-like over the body when at rest, often with a slight gap down the middle where you can see the back

habitat: Round-tipped coneheads thrive in wet, grassy areas throughout New England's lower elevations. Look for them in marshy meadows, soggy roadside ditches, abandoned fields with tall weeds, and the edges of ponds or streams where grasses grow thick. They particularly favor areas where native grasses mix with common weeds like goldenrod and asters.

seasonality.spring: Adults are not present during spring months. Any conehead-like insects seen in spring would be different species or other katydid relatives.
seasonality.summer: Late summer (August) brings the first adults, but they're still developing and may not be at full size or singing regularly yet.
seasonality.fall: Peak season for round-tipped coneheads in September and October when adults are fully mature, actively singing, and most easily found and identified.
seasonality.winter: Adults die off after the first hard frosts, leaving only eggs to survive the winter months buried in soil or plant debris.

funFact: Male round-tipped coneheads are like tiny DJs of the insect world - they can actually change their song tempo based on the temperature, chirping faster on warm nights and slower when it's cool, creating a natural thermometer you can hear!
confusionNotes: Round-tipped coneheads are easily confused with their conehead cousins, especially the sword-bearing conehead. The memory trick: 'Round and blunt won't cut or hunt' - the round-tipped species has a blunt cone that looks like it couldn't cut anything, while sword-bearing coneheads have sharp, pointed cones that look like tiny sword tips.
contextualKnowledge: Despite being called 'coneheads,' these insects aren't related to the comedy characters - their cone is actually a specialized head structure that may help with sound reception or species recognition. The scientific name 'retusus' means 'blunt' or 'rounded off' in Latin, directly referring to their signature rounded cone tip.
compareHints: Among New England's conehead katydids, the round-tipped species stands out for its distinctly blunt head cone, while most relatives like the sword-bearing conehead have sharp, pointed tips. The round-tipped is also typically found in wetter habitats than some of its cousins, and tends to be active later in the season than species like the broad-tipped conehead. Size-wise, it falls in the middle range of the conehead group - not as robust as the aptly-named robust conehead, but larger than the slightly musical conehead.

relatedSpecies.distinction: Among New England's coneheads, the Sword-bearing is distinguished by its sharp, blade-like head tip, while the Round-tipped Conehead has a blunt, rounded projection and the Robust Conehead is noticeably bulkier overall.
